thread.title: Autism & Schizophrenia: Brain Intelligence Genes Found
thread.title_full: Autism & Schizophrenia: Brain Intelligence Genes Found

author: Grace Chen
title: Autism & Schizophrenia: Brain Intelligence Genes Found
text:
Genetic Switch Found to Offer Clues to Human Intelligence,Autism,and Schizophrenia A newly identified genetic sequence may hold the key to understanding what makes humans uniquely bright,while also shedding light on the origins of complex neurological conditions like autism and schizophrenia. Researchers at the University of California – San Diego (UC san Diego) have pinpointed a “promising candidate” – a genetic switch – that appears to regulate brain cell production and could be linked to cognitive flexibility.
Did you know? – The human brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons, each capable of forming thousands of connections. Thes connections, called synapses, are the basis of learning and memory. The brain also contains glial cells,which support and protect neurons.
Five million years ago, the human lineage diverged from that of chimpanzees, initiating a period of rapid evolution.Despite the now-obvious distinctions, pinpointing the specific genetic changes driving this growth has remained a significant challenge. This new finding, published in science Advances , represents a major step forward in unraveling this mystery.
the Search for “Human Accelerated Regions” The research builds upon work initiated in 2006, focusing on identifying human accelerated regions (HARs) – DNA sequences that are highly conserved across mammals but have undergone rapid mutation specifically within the human genome. Scientists established two key criteria for identifying these regions: they must be present in other mammals and remarkably stable over millions of years,yet demonstrate unusually rapid change along the human evolutionary line.
To date, approximately 3,000 HARs have been identified. These sequences,averaging 260 base pairs in length,frequently enough don’t encode genes themselves,but exert a powerful influence on our physiology. They function as transcription amplifiers , essentially acting as “molecular volume controls” that regulate gene expression – dictating which genes are activated, how strongly, and when during development.
HAR123: A Key regulator of Brain development The UC san Diego team has now identified HAR123 as a particularly significant region. While present in the genomes of chimpanzees and mice, HAR123 has evolved rapidly in humans. Their study demonstrates that HAR123 likely plays a crucial role in the development of the human brain.
Pro tip: – When reading scientific papers, pay close attention to the methods section. This section explains how the research was conducted, allowing you to evaluate the validity of the findings. Look for details on sample size,controls,and statistical analyses.
Specifically, HAR123 regulates the production of neuronal progenitor cells (NPCs) – the precursors to both nerve cells and glial cells . Glial cells provide vital support to nerve tissue, ensuring efficient electrical conductivity. HAR123 coordinates the ratio between neurons and glial cells, a balance that profoundly impacts brain development, synaptic function, and neuroplasticity – the brain’s ability to learn.
“It is indeed tempting to speculate that Har123 could promote the formation of cognitive flexibility – the ability to learn and replace previously acquired knowledge,” researchers wrote. This suggests a direct link between this genetic switch and our capacity for complex thought and adaptation.
Implications for Neurological Disorders The critical function of HAR123 – controlling the neuron-to-glia cell ratio – also suggests a potential connection to various neurological diseases and disorders. Imbalances in this ratio have been implicated in conditions such as autism , schizophrenia , alzheimer’s disease , and Parkinson’s disease .
reader question: – How might understanding the role of HAR123 lead to new treatments for neurological disorders? What are your thoughts on the potential for gene editing to correct imbalances in the neuron-to-glia cell ratio? Share your ideas in the comments.
